domain_restrictions: n is an integer and n is at least 2.
The sequence s has exactly n minus 1 entries.
Each entry of s is either plus 1 or minus 1.
The tuple a is a permutation of {1, 2, ..., n}, so all entries are distinct and each integer from 1 to n appears exactly once.
The inequality si times (a(i+1) - ai) greater than 0 means ai+1 is greater than ai when si is plus 1, and ai+1 is less than ai when si is minus 1.
The constraint must hold for every index i from 1 to n minus 1.
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For each integer n at least 2, among all length n minus 1 sequences of plus or minus 1, determine exactly which sign patterns maximize the number of permutations of 1 through n whose consecutive differences have the prescribed signs.
quantifier_order: First fix an integer n with n at least 2.
Then range over all sign sequences s of length n minus 1.
For a given s, count all permutations a of {1, 2, ..., n} satisfying the adjacent sign constraints for every i from 1 to n minus 1.
Finally, for each n, identify which sequences s maximize this count.

payload.theorem_nl: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \\geq 2$. For a sequence $s = (s_1,\\dots,s_{n-1})$ where each $s_i = \\pm 1$, let $f(s)$ be the number of permutations $(a_1,\\dots,a_n)$ of $\\{1,2,\\dots,n\\}$ such that $s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0$ for all $i$. For each $n$, determine the sequences $s$ for which $f(s)$ is maximal.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Refine the count by recording the rank of the last entry of a valid partial permutation. Lemma L1 shows that extending the sign pattern by +1 applies the prefix-sum operator U to this rank-count vector, while extending by -1 applies the suffix-sum operator D. The hard lemma L6, proved by induction on the remaining length using L2 through L5, says that from any monotone nonnegative state the unique best future sign string is alternating, beginning with the sign opposite to the monotonicity direction. After one initial +1 step the state is (0,1), so L6 forces the rest of the pattern to be -1,+1,-1,... and gives uniqueness in the class of patterns starting with +1. Lemma L7 transports this result by termwise sign negation to patterns starting with -1 and shows that the two alternating patterns have equal counts. Hence the global maximizers are exactly the two alternating sign sequences.

steps.derives: If n=2, the two possible sign sequences are (+1) and (-1), each has exactly one valid permutation, so the maximizing sequences are exactly the two alternating sequences of length 1.
steps.trivial_justification: When n=2 there are only two permutations, (1,2) and (2,1). The pattern (+1) is satisfied only by (1,2), and the pattern (-1) is satisfied only by (2,1). Thus both counts are 1, and these are exactly the two alternating sign patterns of length 1.

steps.derives: Assume n>=3 and let s be a sign sequence of length n-1 with first sign s_1=+1. Write t=(s_2,...,s_{n-1}), so t has length n-2. Then f(s)=Total(T_t(x_plus)) where x_plus=(0,1).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 to the sign sequence s. The initial refined vector is v^(1)=(1). Because s_1=+1, the recurrence gives v^(2)=U((1))=(0,1). The remaining signs s_2,...,s_{n-1} act on this state exactly by the iterated operator T_t, and the final total of the resulting vector is f(s).

steps.derives: The vector x_plus=(0,1) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and nonconstant.
steps.trivial_justification: This is immediate from the explicit coordinates 0 and 1.

steps.derives: Still assuming n>=3, among all sign sequences s of length n-1 with first sign +1, the value f(s) is maximized uniquely when t equals Alt_(n-2)^-. Equivalently, the unique maximizer in the class s_1=+1 is the full alternating pattern (+1,-1,+1,-1,...).
steps.trivial_justification: By A1, every sequence with first sign +1 has count f(s)=Total(T_t(x_plus)) for some length-(n-2) suffix t. By A2, x_plus is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and nonconstant. Therefore L6 applies in its nondecreasing case and yields Total(T_t(x_plus)) <= Total(T_(Alt_(n-2)^-)(x_plus)), with equality if and only if t=Alt_(n-2)^-. Appending the fixed initial sign +1 shows that the unique maximizing full pattern in this class is (+1,-1,+1,-1,...).

steps.derives: For every sign sequence s of length n-1 with first sign -1, if s'=-s then s' has first sign +1 and f(s)=f(s').
steps.trivial_justification: The first sign changes from -1 to +1 under termwise negation, and L7 gives f(s)=f(-s)=f(s').

steps.derives: Still assuming n>=3, among all sign sequences of length n-1 with first sign -1, the value f(s) is maximized uniquely by the full alternating pattern (-1,+1,-1,+1,...).
steps.trivial_justification: Take any sign sequence s with first sign -1 and set s'=-s. By A4, f(s)=f(s') and s' starts with +1. By A3, among all patterns starting with +1, the unique maximizer is (+1,-1,+1,-1,...). Therefore s is maximal in the class of patterns starting with -1 exactly when s' is that +1-starting alternating pattern, equivalently when s is its termwise negation (-1,+1,-1,+1,...). Uniqueness is preserved because negation is a bijection on sign sequences.

steps.derives: The two alternating sequences (+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and (-1,+1,-1,+1,...) have the same value of f.
steps.trivial_justification: The second alternating sequence is the termwise negation of the first, so L7 implies their counts are equal.

steps.derives: Assume n>=3. Over all sign sequences of length n-1, the global maximizers of f are exactly the two alternating sequences (+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and (-1,+1,-1,+1,...).
steps.trivial_justification: Every sign sequence starts either with +1 or with -1. By A3, the unique maximizer in the +1 class is the +1-starting alternating pattern. By A5, the unique maximizer in the -1 class is the -1-starting alternating pattern. By A6, these two classwise maxima have the same value, so both are global maximizers and no other sequence can be a global maximizer.

steps.derives: For every integer n at least 2, the sequences s for which f(s) is maximal are exactly the two alternating sign patterns, namely those satisfying s_i s_{i+1} = -1 for every 1 <= i <= n-2; equivalently, s_i = (-1)^(i-1) for all i or s_i = -(-1)^(i-1) for all i.
steps.trivial_justification: A0 handles the case n=2 directly. A7 handles all cases n>=3. The two explicit formulas are exactly the two length-(n-1) sign sequences whose consecutive signs always alternate, so this gives the full characterization demanded in the theorem.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n be an integer at least 2, let s=(s_1,...,s_{n-1}) with each s_i in {+1,-1}, and for each k with 1 <= k <= n define a vector v^(k)=(v^(k)_1,...,v^(k)_k) by declaring v^(k)_j to be the number of permutations b=(b_1,...,b_k) of {1,...,k} such that s_i(b_{i+1}-b_i)>0 for every 1 <= i < k and b_k is the j-th smallest element of {b_1,...,b_k}. Then v^(1)=(1). Moreover, for each k with 1 <= k <= n-1 and each j with 1 <= j <= k+1, with empty sums interpreted as 0, if s_k=+1 then v^(k+1)_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} v^(k)_i, while if s_k=-1 then v^(k+1)_j = sum_{i=j}^{k} v^(k)_i. In particular, if f(s) denotes the number of permutations a=(a_1,...,a_n) of {1,...,n} with s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)>0 for all 1 <= i <= n-1, then f(s)=sum_{j=1}^n v^(n)_j.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: It introduces a finer state space and proves a recurrence, but it does not compare different sign patterns or solve the maximization problem.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be a positive integer, let x=(x_1,...,x_m) be a vector of nonnegative real numbers, and define vectors U(x) and D(x) of length m+1 by U(x)_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} x_i and D(x)_j = sum_{i=j}^{m} x_i for 1 <= j <= m+1, with empty sums interpreted as 0. Then U(x)_1=0, U(x)_{m+1}=x_1+...+x_m, and U(x) is nondecreasing. Also D(x)_1=x_1+...+x_m, D(x)_{m+1}=0, and D(x) is nonincreasing. If at least one entry of x is positive, then both U(x) and D(x) are nonconstant.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: It is a pure statement about elementary sum operators on vectors and contains no permutation counting or optimization over sign patterns.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be a positive integer. Let x=(x_1,...,x_m) be a nonnegative vector and let w=(w_1,...,w_m) be a positive vector with w_1 > w_2 > ... > w_m. If x_1 >= x_2 >= ... >= x_m, then sum_{i=1}^m x_i w_i >= sum_{i=1}^m x_i w_{m+1-i}, and the inequality is strict when x is nonconstant. If x_1 <= x_2 <= ... <= x_m, then sum_{i=1}^m x_i w_{m+1-i} >= sum_{i=1}^m x_i w_i, and the inequality is strict when x is nonconstant.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: It is a standalone rearrangement inequality on finite vectors and is unrelated to permutations except through later applications.

lemmas.statement_nl: Fix positive integers m and r. For a vector x of length m and a sign string t=(t_1,...,t_r) with each t_q in {+1,-1}, define x^(0)=x and for q=1,...,r define x^(q) by x^(q)=U(x^(q-1)) when t_q=+1 and x^(q)=D(x^(q-1)) when t_q=-1, where for any vector y=(y_1,...,y_ell), the vectors U(y) and D(y) of length ell+1 are given by U(y)_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} y_i and D(y)_j = sum_{i=j}^{ell} y_i for 1 <= j <= ell+1, with empty sums equal to 0. Write T_t(x)=x^(r). Let Alt_r^+=(+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and Alt_r^-=(-1,+1,-1,+1,...) be the two alternating sign strings of length r. Then there exists a vector w_{m,r}=(w_1,...,w_m) of positive integers with w_1 > w_2 > ... > w_m such that for every real vector x=(x_1,...,x_m), Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)) = sum_{i=1}^m w_i x_i and Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)) = sum_{i=1}^m w_{m+1-i} x_i, where Total(y) denotes the sum of the entries of y.

lemmas.statement_nl: Fix positive integers m and r. Define U, D, T_t, Total, Alt_r^+, and Alt_r^- exactly as follows: if y=(y_1,...,y_ell), then U(y) and D(y) are length ell+1 vectors given by U(y)_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} y_i and D(y)_j = sum_{i=j}^{ell} y_i for 1 <= j <= ell+1, with empty sums equal to 0; for a sign string t=(t_1,...,t_r), T_t(x) is obtained by applying U or D successively according to the signs; Alt_r^+=(+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and Alt_r^-=(-1,+1,-1,+1,...) have length r; and Total(y) is the sum of the entries of y. If x is a nonnegative nonincreasing vector of length m, then Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)) >= Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)), with strict inequality if x is nonconstant. If x is a nonnegative nondecreasing vector of length m, then Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)) >= Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)), with strict inequality if x is nonconstant.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: It compares only two explicitly specified suffixes and assumes a monotone starting state; it does not optimize over all sign strings from scratch.

lemmas.statement_nl: Fix positive integers m and r. Define U, D, T_t, Total, Alt_r^+, and Alt_r^- exactly as follows: if y=(y_1,...,y_ell), then U(y) and D(y) are length ell+1 vectors given by U(y)_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} y_i and D(y)_j = sum_{i=j}^{ell} y_i for 1 <= j <= ell+1, with empty sums equal to 0; for a sign string t=(t_1,...,t_r) with each t_q in {+1,-1}, T_t(x) is obtained by applying U or D successively according to the signs; Alt_r^+=(+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and Alt_r^-=(-1,+1,-1,+1,...) have length r; and Total(y) is the sum of the entries of y. Let x be a nonnegative vector of length m. If x is nonincreasing, then for every sign string t of length r, Total(T_t(x)) <= Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)). If x is nonconstant, equality holds if and only if t = Alt_r^+. If x is nondecreasing, then for every sign string t of length r, Total(T_t(x)) <= Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)). If x is nonconstant, equality holds if and only if t = Alt_r^-.

candidates.strategy_summary: Encode f(s) by the standard dynamic program that tracks the rank of the last entry. The update for the next sign is either a prefix-sum operator or a suffix-sum operator on the current rank-count vector. Prove a general optimization principle for these operators: from any nonincreasing state, the unique best remaining sign string is the alternating one starting with +1, and from any nondecreasing state, the unique best remaining sign string is the alternating one starting with -1. Starting from the first sign and using the symmetry f(s)=f(-s), this forces the global maximizers to be exactly the two alternating sign patterns.
